claude.reason: A woman taken as collateral in Ashkelon, her family distancing her, witnesses testifying and the Sages ruling: a narrated incident resolved by a ruling.
An incident in which one man sought to give more than a fifth to charity and his friend prevented him: an act met by another person's response.
An exchange between Rabbi and his son, consisting only of speech but with conflict (a challenge and a rebuke to be silent).
A legal dilemma raised by Reish Lakish and left unresolved; no event is narrated.
Rav Yosef ruled in practice according to Rav, and Shmuel took offense and responded sarcastically: an action followed by a reaction, with conflict.
Mar bar Rav Ashi buying a cloth for more than its value is a bare report cited as evidence; nothing follows from it.
Rabbi Eliezer entered a synagogue, found no quorum, and responded by freeing his slave to complete it: a one-time incident with a causal response.
Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy land and Rav bought it for himself: a concrete incident with conflict. The Gemara's justifications are commentary on it.
Reish Lakish sells himself to gladiators, kills his captors, escapes, and later lives without concern for wealth: a full narrative.
A legal objection and answer about fines; no event is narrated.
During a famine the Sages ask Rav Yosef to pray and he refuses: almost entirely speech, but there is tension and a refusal.
A series of legal analogies and objections; no event is narrated.
A girl in Hitlu was assaulted by a dog while sweeping, and Rabbi permitted her to the priesthood: an incident followed by a ruling.
The martyrdom of the woman and her seven sons before the emperor, a post-biblical episode, is a full narrative and in scope.
Rabbi Elazar's ascent, ordination and appointment are events, and he reacts to each one: a short sequence of happenings and responses.
Cases that came before Rabbi and Rabbi Yishmael are only alluded to through their rulings, followed by scholarly discussion; not enough of the incident is given.
Rav Nahman's visit frames a halakhic question-and-answer exchange: speech only, with no real conflict.
Ulla's visit and dialogue with Rav Yehuda about his unmarried son is mostly speech, with some challenge. The interposed exegesis is commentary.
Homa before Rava, Rava going home, and Rav Hisda's daughter driving Homa out of Mehoza: a full narrative with actions and conflict.
A brother promises to share property for a levirate marriage, reneges, and the case passes between rabbis for rulings: an incident resolved by rulings.
Rav Nahman's relative sells her ketubah and dies, the buyers claim it, Rav Nahman's advice is acted on, and he later regrets it.
Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seize an orphans' cow and receive conflicting rulings from Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish: an incident with actions, rulings and conflict.
A pauper eats lentils with Rabbi Nehemya and dies, and Rabbi Nehemya laments: events with a consequence. The Gemara's gloss at the end is commentary.
An incident only alluded to as precedent for a ruling requiring halitza; not enough of it is given.
Rabbi falls ill and is crying, and Rabbi Hiyya enters and questions him: illness, emotion and a visit narrated as an event.
A constructed legal scenario (the Gemara's 'with what are we dealing'), hypothetical rather than an event that happened.
A betrothed couple came before Rava, who placed an intermediary between them; he is challenged and explains his ruling. An incident followed by a ruling.
Legal argument and objection about converts; no narrated event.
Rabbi Yohanan's relatives come to him about a costly medical case, he advises them, then regrets acting as a legal advisor. The Gemara's explanation is commentary.
Rabbi Oshaya stays silent toward Rabbi Yohanan but answers Reish Lakish, and is confronted by Rabbi Yehuda Nesia. There is action (silence, answering another) and social conflict.
A man brings first shearings to Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha, who refuses them, disqualifies himself, appoints judges, and reflects on bribery.
Geneiva, led out to execution, makes a bequest to Rabbi Avina, and Rabbi Zeira rules on it. An incident followed by a ruling; the further legal reasoning is commentary.
A document comes before Rava, Rav Pappa testifies it was paid, Rava rejects him as a single witness, and Rav Adda challenges him. An incident with a ruling.
A pauper used to luxury eats lentils with Rabbi Nehemya and dies; Rabbi Nehemya laments. Clear events and a consequence.
Dama ben Netina's mother tears his cloak, strikes him and spits at him, and he does not shame her. A one-time event about a post-biblical figure.
Mostly speech: Rabbi Yannai rebukes Rav Hanina and sends him out. There is conflict but little action beyond the speech.
Rabbi Elazar teaches without naming Rabbi Yohanan, who grows angry; colleagues fail to appease him and Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi succeeds. Conflict, actions and a resolution.
An inheritance dispute between supposed brothers comes before Rav Hisda, who shifts the burden of proof onto the violent man. An incident followed by a ruling.
Bar Haddaya, bringing a bill of divorce, gets conflicting rulings from Rabbi Ahai and from Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi. An incident followed by rulings.
General dicta about sending a child to school too young; no event.
Rabbi Ami declares a neighbour a mamzer; the man goes about weeping and Rabbi Ami answers him. An event, an emotional reaction and a response.
Reports a habitual practice (meat bought daily for a poor man) with no one-time event after it; the rest is the Gemara's commentary.
A legal objection from a mishna; no narrative.
As Rabbi is dying he summons his sons, who come in, and he gives them his last instructions. A narrated event; segment 3 is the Gemara's commentary.
Abdan's daughters-in-law rebel, Rabbi sends Sages, the women retort, and Rabbi rules. An incident with a ruling; the Gemara's analysis after it is commentary.
Rabba reports finding scholars discussing a legal point and his reply. A scholarly exchange with no event or conflict.
Homiletic teachings about fingers and ears; no narrative.
Mostly a scholarly exchange: Mar Yehuda's challenge silences two scholars, who take it to Rabba, and he rebukes the questioner. There is conflict but only minimal action.
After a man contests a field and dies, his steward argues the orphans' case before Abaye, wins the furrow and the palms, and Abaye praises him. An incident with rulings and a resolution.
The dying Mar Ukva reviews his charity records, judges them insufficient, and gives away half his wealth. The Gemara's legal question about it is commentary.

Rabbi Zeira objects to Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak's dancing; when the old man dies a pillar of fire marks him off, and Zeira reverses his view. The customary dancing is the frame, and one-time events follow it.
These are habitual reports ('when such a person came before him...') cited as evidence of Rav Yehuda's and Rava's rulings. No particular incident is narrated.
A particular incident (Rami bar Hama's sister's marriage contract is lost), the couple come before Rav Yosef, Abaye challenges him, and Rav Yosef rules. This is incident plus ruling.
Rabbi Elazar intends to rule, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim objects. It is mainly speech, but there is conflict and an implied change.
A brief narrated wonder: a fox nested in a turnip, people weighed it and found sixty litra. It is an actual event with actions, close to the accepted eyewitness-wonder type.
A certain man sells his mother's marriage contract, she dies, he contests the sale, and Rami bar Hama and Rava rule. This is incident plus ruling.
Rav Yosef son of Rava's widow comes before Rav Nehemya and asks for allowances one after another, and he grants them. This is an actual incident with a ruling.
Buyers take the orphan's wine, its price rises, and the parties come before Rav Nahman, who rules. This is incident plus ruling.
An incident of a girl raped at the spring, followed by Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri's ruling. It is a story, though it is the Mishnah's copy.
The Gemara's commentary questioning Rabbi Ya'akov's incident, not the incident itself.
Within a legal discussion, Rav Shmuel bar Bisna's interpretation draws Rav Yosef's rebuke 'You disgust me'. It is speech only, with conflict.
Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha's captive son and daughter are paired by their masters, weep through the night, recognize each other at dawn, and die. A full narrative.
A man sells land to Rav Pappa, ends up not needing the money, and Rav Pappa gives the land back. Something happens and a person responds.
A divorcee comes before Shmuel, Rav Dimi tests whether her baby recognizes her, the baby does, and she is told to take her son. The closing Gemara question is a minor appendage.
Dying, Mar Ukva reviews his charity records, judges them too little, and gives away half his wealth. Narrative events with a response.
Rava tells his wife the Sages are gossiping about her, and she answers. It is a speech exchange with conflict and no further action.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi tricks the Angel of Death, jumps into paradise, refuses to return the knife, and meets Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai. A full narrative.
A question put to Rabbi Yehoshua and his answer and testimony. It is speech only, with no real conflict or event.
A hypothetical legal case from a baraita, not a narrated event.
A city's lineage is contested, Rabbi sends Rabbi Romanus to investigate, and Rabbi rules the convert's daughter fit for the priesthood. This is incident plus ruling.
Rami bar Hama's mother writes two deeds, two judges rule opposite ways, and Rav Sheshet confronts Rav Nahman. An incident with rulings and conflict.
After Rabbi Eliezer's death, four Sages come in to refute him and Rabbi Yehoshua rebukes them. It is mostly legal argument in speech, but with conflict.
Rami bar Yehezkel comes to Benei Berak, sees milk and honey mixing, and comments. A brief eyewitness wonder with actual events.
The Sages award Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter-in-law a wine allowance, she blesses them, and they do not answer amen. Incident, ruling, and response.
Ben Yasiyan, travelling overseas, finds a convert married to his brother's wife, confronts him, and is told of Rabbi Akiva's ruling. An actual encounter.
A specific incident (a debtor sells his land, the creditor repossesses one plot, and the purchaser responds with an offer). Something happens to someone and a person responds.
A narrated incident: a blind man is late, a messenger is sent, reports adultery, and Mar Shmuel rules. An incident followed by a ruling.
A report of Rav Yehuda's ruling with only an allusion to 'the incident that took place'. Not enough of the incident is given.

Part of the narrative of Reish Lakish's visit to console the mourner, in which he has his disseminator recite blessings in turn. Abaye's halakhic comment in [4] is commentary and is not part of the story.
Two men quarrel over a city office, come before Rav Yosef, and Rav Adda bar Ahava's question changes the outcome. There is an incident, conflict and a resolution.
Part of the deathbed narrative of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: he summons his sons in turn and transmits his wisdom and the office of Nasi, which are actions beyond speech.
A report of a habitual practice (meat bought daily for a pauper), followed by Gemara discussion. No one responds and nothing follows.
Rav Yosef is sent to collect money, avoids making an acquisition, and Rav Sheshet responds. A concrete incident with a response.
Brief eyewitness recollections cited as evidence for a principle about waiters. Nothing develops.
Two rabbis on a journey see men sowing diverse kinds. The passage is mainly a dialogue in which one proposes ostracism and the other rejects it: conflict with little action.
A dialogue between Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Elazar with disagreement and an emotional reaction (Rabbi Yohanan's grief) that prompts a response. Mostly speech, but with conflict.
Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai meets Nakdimon's impoverished daughter. There are events, an encounter, an emotional reaction (crying) and a resolution.
An incident (a bequest to Toviya, the testator's death, Toviya's arrival) followed by Rabbi Yohanan's ruling. This is R-C0's incident-plus-ruling shape.
Part of a narrative: the sages leave by three exits, Rabbi Akiva meets Yonatan ben Harkinas, withstands his challenges and responds to his angry words. There is action and conflict.
Shmuel is helped off a ferry by a man, learns the man has a case, and disqualifies himself. An event followed by a response.
A deposit is left, the bailee dies, the parties come before Rabbi Ami, and he rules. Segment [3] is the Gemara's qualifying comment, not part of the story.
A Jew and a gentile walking together; the gentile provokes a sigh and then challenges him, and the Jew responds. There are actions, conflict and a resolution.
A rented donkey dies after the renter takes the forbidden path, and the case comes before Rava, who rules (Abaye objects). Incident plus ruling.
A habitual frame (Rabbi Hanina's weekly gift) followed by a one-time event: his wife delivers the money and reports what she overheard.
A man comes before Reish Lakish to testify, and the passage is a dialogue with Rabbi Elazar's objection. There is conflict but little action beyond speech and no resolution.
Halakhic derivations from verses. Shmuel's instruction to Rav Hana is a speech act cited as a precedent, with no event or conflict.

A report of Yitzhak the Exilarch's death raises a legal question, and Abaye cites an incident: a bill of divorce is found, the question is sent to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, and he replies. These are incidents followed by rulings.
Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi is enticed by a noblewoman, disfigures himself, is healed by her magic, flees to a dangerous bathhouse, and is questioned the next day. A full narrative.
Rav Huna bar Avin's sons buy a maidservant with collateral, her price rises, and they come before Rabbi Ami, who rules. Incident plus ruling.

A divorced betrothed couple comes before Rava, who places an intermediary between them, and Rav Adda bar Mattana challenges him. Segment [3] gives an alternative version of the same incident and ruling.
Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy land and Rav bought it for himself; a narrated incident with conflict, followed by the Gemara's justification.
Two narrated incidents: buildings collapse under R. Abbahu and R. Yohanan, they pull up their attendants, and the Sages question R. Yohanan, who responds.
Only the wording of a message Abaye sent. Speech with no event, and the passage alone carries no narrated situation.
An incident (a reservoir found deficient), a dispute between R. Tarfon and R. Akiva over the ruling, and a resolution in which R. Tarfon concedes; an incident followed by a ruling.
Sages reclining in Lod debate whether study or action is greater. Speech only, but with disagreement and a resolution.
A woman obliged to swear an oath, an opposing litigant's demand, her counter-request, and Rav Beivai's ruling: a narrated court incident with a ruling.
A husband gives his first wife's maidservant to his second wife; she cries out before Rava, who ignores her. An incident followed by a response.
The incident is only alluded to ('there was an incident'). We are told the ruling and almost nothing of what happened.
A rumor and a precedent cited only as a legal ruling. Not enough of the incident is told.
Rabbi falls ill, R. Hiyya enters, finds him weeping, questions him, and Rabbi answers. Events plus an emotional reaction.
Rabbi's maidservant immerses, a bone is found between her teeth, and Rabbi requires another immersion: an incident followed by a ruling.
The Yavne reservoir incident, the dispute between R. Tarfon and R. Akiva, and R. Tarfon's acceptance: an incident with a ruling and a resolution.
A man let witnesses trace their names on ordinary documents and Rav Kahana had him flogged. A narrated act, then a response.
A man sold his property to move to Eretz Yisrael, went, could not settle, and Rava ruled on the sale: R-C0's incident-plus-ruling shape.
A gentile's threat, the missing man's wife going to Abaye, his deferral, being sent to Rav Yosef, and his ruling: a multi-step narrated incident.
R. Hananya ben Hakhinai's twelve years away, his return, his wife's death from shock, and her revival through prayer: a full narrative.
R. Elazar b. R. Tzadok's eyewitness account of seeing Nakdimon's daughter gleaning barley, and his reciting a verse over her. A one-line eyewitness account, accepted elsewhere as a story.
The Sages award Nakdimon's daughter a perfume allowance, she blesses them sarcastically, and they answer amen. An incident with a ruling and responses.
R. Simlai's remark to his host is speech only, with no conflict and no event, cited as legal evidence.
R. Asi's relative takes his question to two rabbis, gets conflicting rulings, and R. Asi confronts R. Yohanan. Actions, conflict and resolution.
Rav Hamnuna comes before Rav Huna, who sees his head uncovered, questions him, and turns his face away in rebuke. Action and conflict.
Rav and Rav Yehuda are walking with a woman ahead of them, Rav urges them to hurry away, and they argue. A narrated situation with a response.
A creditor seizes an ox from an orphans' herdsman, the two dispute when it happened, and Rav Nahman rules: incident plus ruling.
A fox nested in a turnip, which they weighed at sixty litra: a brief narrated wonder incident of the kind accepted in Ketubot 111b.
Rav Kahana gathers fallen dates, the owner objects, and Rav Kahana responds by praising R. Yoshiya. An event with conflict and a response.
Abaye's boast and a Sage's challenge are speech only, though the challenge carries some conflict; the rest is a legal exchange.
Rabbi Yohanan's relatives come to him with a case, he advises them, and he later regrets it; an incident with a response and consequence.
A dialogue between an Amorite and a resident of Eretz Yisrael with mockery and retort; speech only, but with conflict.
Rav Aha bar Ya'akov goes to study, is denied lodging, and a miracle kills the demon; a full narrative introduced by the 'like that' formula.
A man bequeathed a palm tree to his daughter and died leaving two halves; a narrated incident that leads to a ruling (R-C0 shape).
Gardeners' calculation, a transfer, the gardener's later discovery and his coming before Rav Nahman for a ruling: an incident followed by a ruling.
A report of the habitual practices of Rav Safra and Rava cited as evidence; nothing follows.
Bare reports of how many blessings Levi and Rav Asi recited at weddings, cited as evidence, with no response or continuation.
Rabbi Yishmael b. R. Yosei, Abdon and Rabbi: a confrontation, a yevama case, and Abdon's punishment; a full narrative.
Rav Amram the Pious is tempted by a captive woman, climbs the ladder, cries out and overcomes his inclination; a full narrative.
Mar Zutra visits the dying convert and acquires his slave; the following debate over the slave's age is the Gemara's commentary.
Homa comes before Rava, her arm is exposed, Rava goes home, and his wife drives Homa out of Mehoza; a full narrative.
A yevama falls to a man, his brother seeks to disqualify her, and they negotiate a property division; an incident that leads to a ruling.
Rabbi Elazar ascends to Eretz Yisrael, is ordained and appointed to the council, and responds to each event; a sequence of events with his reactions.
The fisherman lost in the cave, presumed dead and eulogized, emerges the next day; a narrated incident with Rabbi's response.
Rabba bar Rav Huna teaches, is challenged, and publicly retracts; mostly speech acts with conflict and change (low confidence at most per the register).
A woman from Mehoza married into Neharde'a comes before Rav Nahman, who identifies her accent, rules, is challenged, and revises; an incident with a ruling.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba finds R. Yehoshua b. Levi hurrying his grandson to synagogue, asks why, and changes his own practice from then on.
A man states his town and R. Yitzhak Nappaha states its location; speech only with no conflict, followed by legal discussion.
Aher sees Hutzpit's tongue dragged by a pig, reacts, and goes out to sin; events with a consequence, about a post-biblical figure.
Dama ben Netina's mother tears his cloak, strikes him and spits at him, and he does not shame her; an incident about a post-biblical figure.
A man deposits a goblet with Hasa, Hasa dies, and they come before Rav Nahman for a ruling; an incident followed by a ruling.
Mar Ukva writes about his tormentors, Rabbi Elazar replies, and Geneiva is later put in a neck iron; segment 5 is a separate halakhic query.
Rav Yosef b. Rava leaves his studies for Yom Kippur, his father confronts him armed, and both miss the pre-fast meal; events with conflict and consequence.
R. Yehoshua b. Hananya finds a captive child in Rome, recognizes his wisdom, and ransoms him; he becomes R. Yishmael b. Elisha.
An incident: a half-slave woman's master was forced to free her. Something happens and a court responds; the Gemara's question that follows is commentary.
Rav Ashi first forgets the testimony, then remembers it and testifies. Rav Kahana hesitates and Rav Ashi answers him. There are actions, conflict and a resolution.
A sick Madonite wants to give his property away, is advised, acquires land, makes the gift and dies, and the Sages carry out his words. It is a full incident with a resolution.
A widow sues Rav Hiyya Arikha. There is a ruling, he defies it, there is an appeal to Rava, and she argues with Rava. It is an extended incident with conflict and actions.
A gentile announces that Hasa has drowned and Rav Nahman exclaims. Hasa's wife then remarries and no one protests. An event and a response; Rav Ashi's inference is attached.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Ami's slave immerses a gentile woman, and Rav Yosef rules on her and her daughter. This is an incident followed by a ruling; segments 3-5 are justification and further precedent.
A couple disputes the bride's virginity before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi. He has the cloth laundered, finds blood and rules. There are actions and a resolution.
A purely legal discussion of the claim 'I found an open orifice'. Nothing happens to anyone.
In Neresh a betrothed bride is seized by another man, and Rav's students do not require a divorce from him. An incident followed by a ruling; segment 3 is the Gemara's explanation.
A husband spends his own money collecting his wife's inheritance and uses one of her dinars. He comes before Rabbi Ami, who rules, the Rabbis challenge it, and he revises the ruling.
A scholarly exchange: an objection and an answer passed down a chain of tradents. It is speech with no event and no real conflict.
A man in a synagogue tells those present to write a divorce, and then the schoolteacher dies. An incident that leads to disputed rulings and a final halakha.
Mostly dialogue between Geneiva and Rav Huna and Rav Hisda, with little action beyond approaching and declining food. There is tension over whether to honor an argumentative man.
Only the man's two statements are given, as the facts of a legal question. Too little of an incident and no event beyond speech.
Elijah visits Rav Anan, leaves after his wrongdoing and returns after fasting and prayer, but frightens him. Rav Anan builds a box to keep learning. This is in scope as Elijah appearing to a rabbi.
Fire breaks out at a wedding and the bride cries out. People find a burnt body and a hand. Segment 3 is the legal analysis.
In two short incidents a litigant does a small favor for a judge, and the judge (Ameimar, then Mar Ukva) recuses himself. In each, an action draws a response.
The incident is only alluded to (Rabbi gave one-twelfth) and cited as evidence inside a legal argument.
Rav Hisda's daughter tells Rava that a woman obligated to take an oath is suspect, and Rava reverses the oath onto the other party. An incident with a response.
Beloreya's slaves immerse before she does, the case comes before the Sages, and they rule the slaves free. Incident plus ruling; the rest is Rav Hisda's inference.
In a court case over a woman's oath, Rav Beivai orders a document written and Rav Pappi sharply rebukes him. There is conflict and action.
Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi is enticed by a noblewoman, afflicts himself, is healed by her magic, flees to a dangerous bathhouse and is protected. A full story; the closing teaching is commentary.
Rabbi Hanina's wife finds that the pauper he supports lives lavishly, and he responds with Rabbi Elazar's saying. An event and a reaction.
The Sages add cups to the mourners' meal, people get drunk, and the Sages restore the old practice. An event and a response, though it is close to institutional history.
During a famine a couple come before Rabbi over the virginity claim. He has them bathed and fed, blood is then found, and he rules and quotes a verse.

Rabbi Ya'akov ben Dostai's first-person account of a one-time event (walking ankle-deep in honey), with eyewitness wonders following. This is the one-line eyewitness wonder shape the expert accepted in review.
Yehuda bar Mareimar is pressed into the visit, stays silent, Abba of Sura misreads it and writes over all his property, then a dialogue resolves it. Real actions, conflict and change.
Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebels, the sages rule on it, and Rav Gamda rebukes them for flattery. An incident with a ruling and a response.
Rav Hamnuna is sent to Rav Huna, who sees his uncovered head, learns he is unmarried, and turns his face away in rebuke. Action, conflict and consequence.
Rav Kahana is tempted, throws himself from the roof, is caught by Elijah and given money. It is about a rabbi, so Elijah's appearance keeps it in scope.
A man is faced with a levirate obligation abroad, comes to Rabbi Hanina, and gets a sharp ruling. This is the incident-plus-ruling shape, though thin and mostly speech.
A legal discussion that only alludes to the David and Bathsheba incident. Nothing is narrated, and the incident is biblical in any case.
A baraita dispute plus a bare report that Rabbi ruled like Rabbi Ya'akov. No incident is narrated.
Rav takes leave of Rabbi Hiyya with a cryptic blessing, searches and finds the verse, and his wife persistently thwarts his requests. Narrated events with conflict.
A divorcee comes before Shmuel. Rav Dimi tests her by passing her child along a row of women, the child recognizes her, and she is ordered to nurse. The closing question is Gemara commentary.
Segments 2-3 are dicta. Segment 4 is a speech-only exchange where the sages reproach ben Azzai for not marrying and he answers. Conflict but no action, so borderline.
A woman rebels, Mar Zutra compels her to stay, and Rabbi Hanina of Sura is born of the couple. An incident with a ruling and an outcome, though brief.
A man claims shared pure food became impure, the owner comes before Rabbi Ami, who rules, and Rabbi Asi challenges him. An incident followed by a ruling and a dispute.
A marriage contract is brought before Rabbi Abbahu, he means to validate it, and Rabbi Yirmeya objects. An incident with a ruling and a response, though thin.
Reports of sages' practice and opinion on orla outside the Land, cited as evidence. Nothing follows from them.
Ulla disparages Rav Hamnuna's lineage, Hamnuna is ashamed, and Ulla questions him and reverses the slur. Emotion, conflict and resolution.
A pauper asks Rava for rich food, they argue, then Rava's sister arrives with exactly that food and Rava concedes. Events with conflict and change.
A man recalls being immersed as a child to eat teruma, and Rabbi elevates him to the priesthood on that statement. An incident with a ruling.
Marta bat Baitos sends her agent repeatedly for flour, goes out herself and dies, and Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai applies a verse to her. A full narrative about post-biblical figures.
Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa and the Angel of Death, the pillar of fire at his death, and Rabbi Alexandri dispelling it. A full narrative with action and conflict.
Rabbi Ya'akov ben Dostai's first-person account of a one-time event (walking ankle-deep in honey), with eyewitness wonders following. This is the one-line eyewitness wonder shape the expert accepted.
The parents dispute the match, the father is pressured into agreeing, and during the meal his relative betroths the girl on the roof. Segment 3 is the Gemara's analysis and is excluded.
A woman seizes a silver cup toward her ketubah, demands sustenance, and Rava orders the orphans to pay. An incident followed by a ruling.
A legal objection quoting a mishna dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about hypothetical cases. No narrated event.
A man deposits pearls with Rabbi Meyasha, who dies without instructions, and Rabbi Ami rules for the depositor. An incident followed by a ruling.
Rav Nahman's arrival only frames a halakhic exchange of questions and answers; speech with no event beyond it and no real conflict.
A widow comes before Rav Nehemya with claims and he apportions sustenance and wine for her: an actual incident resolved by a ruling.
A bare report that Rav Yehuda acted in a case of branches, cited as evidence of his view; the incident is only alluded to.
A full story about Nebuzaradan and Zechariah's blood, biblical-era characters; the expert ruled this passage out of scope.
Mostly a proposal and a response among the Sages, with only the outbreak of trouble interrupting; speech with some conflict over the earlier rival wives.
Rabbi Zeira crosses by rope and a Sadducee mocks him; essentially a dialogue whose conflict is mockery, which the expert ruled borderline.
An actual incident: Mar Zutra compelled a rebellious wife, and Rabbi Hanina of Sura was born of the couple; an act with a consequence.
The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin buy a maidservant with collateral, her price rises, and Rabbi Ami rules; incident followed by a ruling.
Incidents are only alluded to as precedents (he apportioned / did not), followed by legal discussion among the Amoraim.
A report of Rav Kahana's practice in holding an orphan's beer, with his rationale; nothing follows.
Legal discussion of a deathbed gift; no narrated event.
Ravin went to betroth a woman for his son and betrothed her himself; an actual incident with a turn, the Gemara's justification being commentary.
Ravina simply asks Rav Ashi whether he may take the orphan's wine along and receives an answer; a halakhic consultation with no event or conflict.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi tricks the Angel of Death and enters paradise; segment 2 is a list of practices rather than the story.
A legal exchange about slaughtering a deer on a Festival; pure argument.
The bathhouse and the stair collapse beneath Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yohanan, who pull their supporters up; events with a response.
Rav Huna deliberately tears silk before his son to test whether he will become angry; an actual incident, with the Gemara's objections as commentary.
King Agrippa, a post-biblical figure, yielded to a bride's procession and the Sages praised him; an act followed by a response.
A yevama refuses her yavam before Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, who tricks the yavam into halitza; conflict, actions, resolution.
Mishnaic law on a wife's tasks; no narrative.
Habitual dancing before brides, criticized by Rabbi Zeira, followed by the one-time event of the pillar of fire at Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak's death.
Rav Pappa goes to write his son's ketuba and Yehuda bar Mareimar escorts him then tries to leave; actions opening a narrative.
A certain man's brother tries to disqualify their yevama by divorce and the two negotiate over the property; an actual incident with conflict.
An agent cannot find the intermediary, three Sages take his agency, Rav Safra objects and they are embarrassed; Rava and Rav Ashi's assessments are commentary.
Yehuda bar Mareimar is pressed to enter, sits silent, and Abba of Sura writes over all his property; actions, conflict and resolution.
A habitual practice of Rav Huna cited as precedent; no one-time event follows and nothing develops.
Two incidents where something happened to a person and rabbis responded with rulings, including Rav Pappi's sharp rebuke of Rav Beivai.
A recollection of a question and answer with Rav Ashi; speech only, with no event and no real conflict.
A document from Shmuel's court is cited as evidence in a legal discussion; no narrated incident.
Rabbi Hanina's habitual charity followed by a one-time event: his wife delivers it, discovers the pauper's wealth, and reports back.
A one-line report of what Rava did, cited as precedent, with no continuation.
A dialogue with no action beyond speech, but with a mocking challenge and retort, so there is conflict.
Ravina finding Rav Nahman pondering a dilemma is a frame for a halakhic question; nothing happens.
The prince's household seizes the orphans' maidservant, judges sit on the case, and Rabbi Abba challenges them for favoritism: an incident with conflict and a response.
Rabbi's deathbed instructions, his returns home after death that stop after the neighbor episode, and his attendants dying before him; the Gemara's legal glosses (3-5, 9) are commentary.
Rav Ashi's historical account of a court changing an ordinance; an institutional explanation, not a narrated incident about specific people.
A certain man's millstone rental leads to a dispute when circumstances change; the following comparison to the mishna is legal discussion.
A report of Rav Kahana's practice with an orphan's beer and his reasoning; no one responds and nothing follows.
Rav Nahman's relative sells her marriage contract, is divorced and dies; the buyers claim from her daughter and Rav Nahman intervenes with advice.
A 'certain man' incident (an attempted betrothal over thrown dates) followed by Rav Zevid's ruling.
A couple comes before Rav Nahman; he recognizes the woman's accent, rules, is challenged, and reverses his ruling.
The Gemara only alludes to the Tzaidan incident in order to ask why it was cited; the incident is not narrated here.
A yevama spits out of order before Rabbi Ami; Rabbi Abba disputes it, suspects evasion, then goes and verifies; incident, conflict and resolution.
A general custom and halakhic rules, with no specific event.
Rav Yehuda's hearing before Rav Nahman, the litigant's confrontation, Rav Mattana's arrival, the proclamation, and the attempted stoning: a full narrative.
Rabbi's son's match: the bride dies, the families' lineage is investigated, and a new match is made in which the son changes his terms and is ashamed before his father.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi's wife disguises herself and tests him; he sins in intent, sits in the oven, and fasts until his death.
A witness narrates the encounter with the troop and the lion-named man's death, and Rabbi Tarfon allows the wife to remarry.
A virginity dispute before Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi, resolved by his wine-barrel test and ruling.
Agents sent for a silver vessel are menaced by its holders; one gives in, and Rabbi Ahai questions and then vindicates him.
A report that Rabba acted in line with his own ruling, cited as evidence for his view. The details are disputed and nothing follows.

Rav Giddel's land is bought out from under him, complaints are passed up the chain, there is a confrontation, and the land is left as 'land of the Sages': a chain of actions with conflict and a resolution.
After a habitual frame comes a one-time event: the sharecropper comes early, Rabbi Yishmael refuses the gift, seats other judges, and reacts inwardly.
Avimi's habitual honoring of his father is followed by a one-time event: he stands over his dozing father until he wakes, and is rewarded.
A description of Rav Ashi's blessing practice, cited for the halakha, with no response and no continuation.
A man brings a claim and Rabban Gamliel answers with a parable. It is almost entirely speech, but there is conflict over the claim.
An incident is only alluded to, in a legal discussion of its facts. Not enough of the incident is given.
A man takes the orphans' coral at his own valuation, it rises in value, and he comes before Rabbi Ammi, who rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
A report of Rav Ashi's practice with the wedding blessings, cited for the halakha, where nothing happens and no one responds.
Rabbi Zekharya testifies to what happened during the siege and the Sages rule against him: an incident followed by a ruling. It is a Mishnah story.
A man sells land to Rav Pappa, then no longer needs the money, and Rav Pappa returns the land: something happens and a person responds.
An incident in Rav Hisda's study hall is only alluded to; the passage is a legal derivation from a mishna.
A court incident: the litigant demands that the woman swear in the town, she makes a counter-demand, Rav Beivai rules, and Rav Pappi rebukes him.
At the wedding feast Rabban Gamliel serves the sages, Rabbi Eliezer refuses the cup, Rabbi Yehoshua accepts, and a dispute follows. Abraham appears only as an exemplum inside a rabbinic story.
A scribe confesses a flaw to Rabbi Ami, who rules on it and then defends the ruling to Rabbi Yirmeya: an incident followed by a ruling.
A description of Mar Zutra's practice, an objection, and a halakhic ruling. The narrative has no continuation.
After a habitual frame comes a one-time event: Rav Rehumi stays away, his wife weeps, the roof collapses and he dies.
In two incidents a man does a judge a small favor, and the judge, on learning he has a case, disqualifies himself: action and response.
Shimon HaAmasoni's habitual exegesis is followed by a one-time event: he reaches one verse and withdraws, his students challenge him, and he responds.
A single sentence of background (who was married to whom), with no event in the passage itself.

Rav Giddel's land is bought out from under him, complaints are passed up the chain, there is a confrontation, and the land is left as 'land of the Sages': a chain of actions with conflict and a resolution.
Two sages intend to rule and are rebuked. It is speech and intention only, with conflict and an implied change.
Yehuda bar Mareimar is pressed to enter and sits silent; Abba of Sura misreads the silence and writes over all his property, and an exchange follows: actions, a misunderstanding and its consequence.
Floors collapse under Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yohanan, each saves his attendants, and the sages question Rabbi Yohanan: events with a response.
Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai escapes Jerusalem and meets Vespasian, a full narrative. Segments 11-12 are the Gemara's commentary and explanation, so they are excluded.
Levi intended to rule by a baraita and Rav corrected him; it is almost all speech, with some disagreement and an implied change (Levi does not act).
A certain man threw what he called a bill of divorce, a mezuza was found, and Rav Nahman ruled. This is an incident followed by a ruling.
Abaye boasts and a scholar challenges him in an exegetical dialogue. It is speech only, but with conflict.
Giddul bar Re'ilai sends a get, his wife puts the agent off, the agent reports back and Giddul reacts with a blessing. These are actions with consequences.
Rabbi Akiva's students all die for lack of mutual respect, the world is desolate, and Akiva goes south and teaches new students who uphold the Torah. These are narrated events with change.
Rabbi Hama bar Bisa returns after twelve years, fails to recognize his son, is distressed, stands before him, and his wife remarks on it. Actions, emotion and resolution.
A deposit dispute over sesame between two men comes before the Sages, and Rav Hisda and Rava rule on it. This is an incident followed by a ruling.
Rav Ilish is taken captive, hears the birds, eavesdrops on Rav Nahman's daughters and escapes, while his companion is killed. A full narrative.
A legal discussion of hypothetical consecration cases. Nothing here happened.
Two deeds come before Rav Yosef, he rules, and the losing party protests and asks for a further document. This is an incident with a ruling and a response.
Rabbi Akiva sees a ship sink and grieves for Rabbi Meir, then finds him alive in Cappadocia and hears how he survived. A first-person narrated event.
A halakhic objection and a resolution about hypothetical cases. No event is narrated.
Abaye's and Rav Sheshet's practices are bare reports. Rav Hanan's visit to Rav Kahana is a small incident, but its substance is a challenge and an answer, so it is speech with only mild conflict.

Testimony cases come before Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yohanan and are ruled on, and Reish Lakish then looks harshly at Rabbi Elazar and rebukes him. Incidents with rulings, an emotional reaction and conflict.
A man brings Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing, and he refuses it, appoints judges, and reflects on how even this biased him. Actions with consequence and inner reaction.
Akiva's habit of mocking sinners is the frame, and the one-time event follows: Satan appears as a woman, Akiva climbs the tree and Satan releases him.
The Mishnah's incident in Sidon: a tanner dies, his brother the tanner is the levir, and the Sages rule that the widow may refuse. An incident with a ruling, located in the Mishnah.
A man wills a palm tree to his daughter, the orphans divide the estate without giving it to her, and Rav Yosef and Abaye rule. An incident with a ruling.
A man wills his property to Toviya and dies, Toviya comes, and Rabbi Yohanan rules. Brief, but an incident followed by a ruling.
Rabbi Hiyya teaches a ruling publicly, in two attributions, and the audience reacts differently to each. A small incident with a response, cited mainly as evidence for the halakha.
The incident of the widow at the grave is only alluded to in the Hebrew text. Not enough of it is given to be a story.
A co-owner frees his half of a slave, the other transfers the slave to his minor son to evade the court, and Rav Pappa devises a counter-ruling. An incident, a response and a ruling.
The letter carries an incident: a man in love wished to leave the Land, heard this teaching, and stayed, suffering until his death. The rest of the letter is advice.
A man brings a claim to Rabban Gamliel, who answers with a suspicion and a parable. It is speech only, with some conflict and no resolution narrated.
Rabbi goes to study with Rabbi Elazar ben Shamua, the students gang up on him, and he learns only one teaching. An event with conflict and an outcome.

Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef meets Rabbi Abbahu, asks who taught the Usha ordinance, then learns it forty times. Mostly speech with a little action and no real conflict, so it sits at the edge of the category.
A report that a problem stayed unsolved for 22 years until Rav Yosef solved it, given as a lead-in to the legal answer. Nothing happens to anyone and no one responds.
A specific bill of divorce dated by the governor of Bascar is sent to Rabba, and he rules on it: an actual incident resolved by a ruling.

A history of the priestly court changing its ordinances as people reacted. There is action and response, but it is a group history of legislation rather than an incident that happened to particular people.
A particular betrothed couple come before Rav Yosef with a dispute over paternity: the start of an incident that ends in a ruling.
A particular man who sold himself to gladiators comes to Rabbi Ami asking to be redeemed: the start of an incident that ends in a ruling.
A poor man eats lentils with Rabbi Nehemya and dies, and Rabbi Nehemya laments: a clear chain of events with a result.
A man buys land near Jerusalem, gives away his property through it, and dies, and the Sages uphold his gift: an incident followed by a ruling.
A question written into a letter and a short exchange between Rabbi and Rabbi Hiyya. It is speech only, with no conflict.
The Gemara's discussion of an incident it only mentions in passing. Nothing is narrated here.
Sages are brought a huge peach; a year later Rabbi Elazar comes, holds a small one in his hand, and responds with a verse: events over time with a reaction.
Giddel bar Re'ilai pays the land tax in advance, the owners come back, and the case goes to Rav Pappa, who is corrected by Rav Huna: an incident with a ruling.
This is the expert's ruled case, Ketubot 15a:0: a legal discussion of the facts of an incident and their consequences, with not enough of the incident given.
A baraita's hypothetical legal case ('if one's bread was baked... and the father died'), not an event that happened.
Rabbi Yehuda of India, a convert with no heirs, falls ill; Mar Zutra visits and moves to acquire his slave as he is dying: an actual incident with consequences.
The habitual practices of two pious men and whether Elijah spoke with each. No one-time event follows the custom.
The death of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: the decreed fast, the maidservant throwing the jug, bar Kappara bringing the news, and his last prayer. A full narrative.
A particular man betroths a woman with a myrtle mat, changes what the betrothal is for, she is silent, and Rava rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
A launderer who missed Rabbi's funeral throws himself from a roof, and a Divine Voice promises him the World-to-Come: events with a resolution.
A purely legal argument between Rav Pappa and Rav Pappi, with no event.

Rav Pappa's sister-in-law's levirate case before Abaye, the ruse, the 'I was fooling you' ruling, and Abaye's gaze that kills Rav Pappa's parents. Segments 4-5 are legal argument embedded in the incident.
Onkelos, a post-biblical figure, raises the dead by necromancy before converting: a narrative in scope. Segment 7 is a separate baraita about Kamtza, not part of this story.
The case of Pishon the camel driver is only alluded to, as evidence in an argument between the Houses. Not enough of the incident is given.
A particular man testifies before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, is questioned, and the other man is raised to Levite status: an incident followed by a ruling and an action.
A drought in Neharde'a leads everyone to sell their mansions, wheat then arrives, and Rav Nahman rules the sales void: an incident followed by a ruling.
A specific person came before Rav Yosef, who ruled; Abaye challenged and Rav Yosef clarified. An actual incident followed by a ruling.

Segment 2 closes the Hanina bar Pappi incident (angels guarded him, sages respond); segment 3 is the full Rabbi Tzadok story with actions, conflict and resolution. The baraita/verse in 2 is commentary.
A man deposited silk, Rav Dimi died, the claimant came before Rabbi Abba who ruled: an incident followed by a ruling.
Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seized the orphans' cow, went back and forth between Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish, with conflict and a resolution.
Rabbi Hama bar Bisa returns after twelve years, meets his son unrecognized, stands before him, and his wife comments; a full narrative. Rami bar Hama's verse at the end is commentary.
After a habitual practice of expounding every 'et', a one-time event follows: he withdrew at a particular verse, his students challenged him and he replied, a change with conflict.
The passage is only the opening words of an incident whose content lies outside it; nothing is narrated within the passage.
Rabbi Yirmeya dozes while two students discuss, wakes up and rebukes them as 'children' with a ruling: actions beyond speech plus conflict. Rav Hisda's statement in 6 is separate discussion.
Legal statements and a baraita giving a hypothetical case ('if one's bread was baked...'); no actual event is narrated.
Ze'eiri avoids Rabbi Yohanan, carries him across water one day, and Rabbi Yohanan confronts him about marrying his daughter: actions, conflict and dialogue.
A one-line report that Rava coerced Rav Natan bar Ami to give charity, cited as a precedent with nothing further narrated.
Shmuel is helped off a ferry by a man who then reveals he has a case, and Shmuel disqualifies himself: an event with a response.
A narrated incident (Levites, sick companion, innkeeper's testimony, wife allowed to remarry). It sits in the Mishnah, so per R-C1 it belongs to the Mishnah, but it is a story.
A steward comes before Abaye and argues the orphans' case successfully through several rounds, ending with Abaye's praise: an incident with rulings.
Marta bat Baitos brought dinars to King Yannai until he appointed Yehoshua ben Gamla: an act that leads to a consequence, involving post-biblical figures.
A man testifies before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, is questioned, and the rabbi elevates the other man to Levite status: an incident followed by a ruling.
A man who sold himself to gladiators asks Rabbi Ami to redeem him; the Sages object and Rabbi Ami ultimately sends him away: conflict and an outcome.
A baraita incident: a witness recounts the lion-hearted traveler's feat and death, Rabbi Tarfon cross-examines him and permits the wife to remarry.
Pure legal analysis of konamot and liens; no event is narrated.
Rabbi Yohanan's relatives seek advice about their stepmother, then Reish Lakish rules against them and threatens them, and Rabbi Yohanan concedes: conflict and actions.
A man set a thirty-day condition, arrived but was blocked by the ferry and shouted that he had come; Shmuel ruled. An incident followed by a ruling.
A baraita incident: a boat carrying two scholars sank, and Rabbi permitted their wives to remarry on women's testimony. Something happened and a ruling followed.

An agent prevented from waiting comes before Rava, who rules; the Sages challenge him, he is embarrassed, and later it emerges the woman was only betrothed: conflict, an emotional reaction, and an outcome.
A brief report that the family remained in Sura and the Sages avoided it, followed by the Gemara's explanation of why; an aftermath remark with no narrative of its own.
Rav objects, Shmuel's father falls silent, and Rav applies a verse to him: speech and silence only, but with clear conflict.
A certain man dies in debt; the creditor repossesses, the orphans redeem, he repossesses again, and Abaye rules. An incident followed by a ruling.
A man sets a condition on a divorce, tries to appease his wife and fails, and Rav Yosef rules (two versions). A narrated incident resolved by a ruling.
Rabbis visit a sick Rabba bar bar Hana; a Persian priest comes in and takes the lamp, and Rabba reacts. A one-time sequence of events.
Beit Hillel's ruling on Queen Helene is only alluded to, as a proof about terminology. Not enough of the incident is told.
Rav Pappa intends to rule, is challenged in a dispute, and holds back. It is almost all dialogue, with conflict and an implied change.
Letters and messengers pass between Rav Anan and Rav Huna. There is conflict, an affront, and people going to others in turn.
A woman comes before Rav Yosef claiming a birth after ten years; he rebukes her and she confesses. Something happened and a rabbi responds.
Two brief first-person reports of being given food at a meal, cited as evidence for a rule, with nothing following.
Rabbi Zeira's sermon gets him pelted with etrogim; Rava preaches, is carried on silk, then preaches again and is challenged. A sequence of events with conflict.
A baraita on yields, then a Sadducee's remark praising his land. Speech only, with no conflict and no event.
A Madonite wants to give gifts, is advised, buys land, makes the gift and dies, and the Sages carry out his words. A narrated incident.
A man betroths with a stone, Rav Hisda assesses it, and the mother objects and is answered. An incident with a ruling and a dispute.
Rav Aha bar Abba visits and puts his granddaughter on his lap; Rav Hisda challenges him and he answers. An action followed by a dispute.
The Sages award Nakdimon's daughter a perfume allowance, she replies with a barbed blessing, and they answer amen. A one-time incident with a response.
Mar Ukva's habit of anonymous charity is the frame; one day the pauper comes out, they flee into a furnace, and his wife consoles him. A full story.
A history of marriage-contract practice: a repeated problem and a series of ordinances, ending in Shimon ben Shatah's enactment. The habitual frame leads to one-time events.
A Mishnah ruling and a sermon given at Yavne. A speech act with no event or conflict.
A rumor spreads that a woman was betrothed; the case is sent to Abaye, who rules to suppress it. An incident followed by a ruling.
Orphans' property is held by Rabbi Banai; they come before Shmuel, who orders support. A short incident with a ruling.
A man mortgages an orchard that ages; the creditor comes before the Sages and they write him a repossession document. An incident followed by a ruling.
Rav Yosef son of Rava leaves study early to go home; his father meets him with a weapon, they quarrel, and both miss the pre-fast meal.
Rav Ashi at first does not recall, later remembers and testifies, and reassures a hesitant Rav Kahana. A sequence of events.
A debtor sells two plots; the creditor repossesses one and comes for the other, and the buyer goes to him with an offer. A narrated incident.
A widow comes before Rav Yosef and asks for maintenance, wine and silk, answering him sharply. Mostly speech and quasi-speech, with some tension.
A man comes before Rav Nahman with a claim, and Rav Nahman orders him flogged, inferring his misconduct. An incident with a ruling.
Ilfa hangs from a ship's mast vowing to drown if he cannot answer; an old man challenges him and he succeeds. Actions, conflict and resolution.
A narrated incident in Shihin: a man inherits mustard stalks, one breaks, yields nine kav, and its wood roofs a booth. Several events happen, plus an eyewitness wonder.
Rav Hamnuna teaches, the audience clamors, and Rav Yosef and Rav Hamnuna talk it out. Almost all speech, but there is conflict and a resolution.
Purely legal discussion of a baraita; no events are narrated.
Rav Hiyya bar Adda is delayed three days harvesting a miraculous vine, and Reish Lakish reproaches him. Events, conflict and consequence.
Shmuel's father posts guards over captive women; later Shmuel's own daughters are taken captive, outwit their captors in Rabbi Hanina's court, and are permitted to marry.
After a habitual frame, one day the sharecropper comes early; Rabbi Yishmael refuses the gift and recuses himself, then notices his own bias. Events and change.
Relatives bring a complaint about the steward Amram to Rav Nahman, who answers each charge. The exchange has conflict but is mostly speech, and its tail is legal commentary.
A groom complains to Rabbi; Rabbi has the famine-starved couple fed and bathed, blood is found, and he rules. Incident, actions and resolution.
A legal analysis that explains a custom by an alleged government decree; no specific incident is narrated.
The people of Bei Mikhsi are seized by gentile creditors and come to Rav Huna, who refuses to redeem them and defends that against Rabbi Abba. An incident followed by a ruling.
Purely legal dictum and analysis about converting a minor.
An incident is only alluded to as precedent for a ruling; not enough of it is told.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov goes to study, Abaye arranges for him to sleep in the study hall, and Rav Aha kills the seven-headed demon. A full narrative.
Ravnai quotes Shmuel, Ameimar praises the ruling and Rav Ashi rebukes him. Essentially speech, with some conflict.
A man betroths with a myrtle branch in the market, the case is sent to Rav Yosef, and he orders the man flogged and a divorce. An incident followed by a ruling.
A man is pierced by a thorn while climbing a palm and later fathers children; Shmuel sends the case to Rav, who orders an inquiry. An incident with a response, cited inside a legal argument.
Conclusion of an incident: his friends shun him and Rabbi elevates him to the priesthood on his word. Events with a resolution.
After the habitual frame comes a one-time event: Abaye rides by, the rabbis do not stand, he challenges them and they reply. Action and conflict.
Rabbi Yehuda bars Rabbi Meir's students, Sumakhos forces his way in, Yehuda grows angry and Yosei responds. Actions, emotion and conflict.
Ulla dies outside the Land; Rabbi Elazar reacts, is told the coffin is coming, and responds. An event and reactions.
A man wills a palm tree to his daughter but leaves two half-trees; the case is debated and resolved by Rava's tradition. An incident followed by a ruling.
Rav Hiyya bar Abba's child dies and Reish Lakish comes with his disseminator to comfort him over several speeches. Segments 3, 4 and 7 are the Gemara's commentary, so they are left out.
The Mishnah's incident is only cited by its title, and the rest is Rav's legal derivations from it.
A man's brother dies abroad, leaving a yevama, and the man comes to Rabbi Hanina, who rebukes the brother and tells him not to go. An incident followed by a ruling.
Continuation of a baraita prescribing procedure for a hypothetical case (if a parent dies before the wedding) plus Gemara qualification; no event that happened.
A certain man set a condition on a divorce, was blocked by the ferry and called out; Shmuel ruled. An incident followed by a ruling.
Rabbi Zeira crosses the Jordan on a rope, a Sadducee mocks him and he answers: action, conflict, and response.
Two men quarrel over a city post, come before Rav Yosef, Rav Adda bar Ahava argues, and the posts are divided; Abaye's moral closes it.
Orphan girls come before Shmuel over property Rabbi Banai held, and he orders them supported: an incident and a ruling. Segment 3 is Gemara analysis.
Two rabbis rise as Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passes, and he responds to them: an event with a reaction.
Rav Asi's elderly mother, his departure, the consultations with Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Elazar, and her coffin arriving: a full narrative.
Rav Nahman arrives in Sura, is asked a legal question, and answers from a mishna; only speech, with no conflict and nothing following.
Incidents in which a gentile reports Jews dead and buried, and the Sages let the wives remarry: events followed by rulings.
A man brings a bill of divorce to Rabbi Yishmael, who rules; Rabbi Elai challenges him afterwards and is silenced: an incident with a ruling and a conflict.
Shmuel's father guards captive women; later Shmuel's own daughters are captured, outwit their captors in court, and are married off: a full narrative.
A bathhouse and a stair collapse under Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yohanan, who pull their helpers up; the Sages question them and get an answer: events with responses.
An agent pays a debt, the creditors refuse to return the document, and Rabbi Abbahu rules: an incident, a conflict and a ruling.
The Sages apportion wine to Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter-in-law, she blesses them, and they decline to answer amen: an incident with a response.
Legal discussion of defects in a slave sale; no narrative.
Academic argument over a halakha and the reconciliation of sources; speech only, with no event.
A man snatches a belt from a woman, makes betrothal conditional on its return, she takes it in silence, and Rav Nahman rules: an incident and a ruling.
A dialogue about a wedding custom, plus a brief report of someone smearing oil at a wedding, cited only as evidence of the practice; nothing follows from it.
A bare note that Rabbi was moved to Tzippori when ill, embedded in source analysis; no narrative development.
Halakhic debate over Rav and Shmuel's rulings; no event.
First-person recollections of being given food, cited as evidence for a rule about waiters; they are reports with no development.
Funeral costs drive families to abandon their dead until Rabban Gamliel is buried in plain linen and everyone follows him: a problem, an action, and a change.
A virginity dispute brought to Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi, his test with maidservants and a wine barrel, and his ruling: a full incident.
A habitual frame (Yehuda's weekly return and the pillar of fire) followed by a one-time event: he is delayed, Rabbi Yannai declares him dead, and he dies.
Mar Ukva's yearly gift (the habitual frame), then one occasion when his son reports the pauper's luxury and Mar Ukva doubles the gift.
A certain person came before Rav Yosef, who ruled and was challenged by Abaye: a narrated incident resolved by a ruling.
Eyewitness account of a woman coming before Ameimar, the brothers' response and his silence: a real incident with a reaction, cited as evidence.
A halakhic exchange between Rava bar Rav Hanan and Abaye; speech only, no narrated event.
A remedy plus a one-line report of a goat with no spleen, cited as corroboration; nothing follows.
The death of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: the decree, the maidservant's prayer and jug, bar Kappara's announcement; a full narrative.
A get is found in Rav Huna's court, Rav Huna rules, Rav Hisda sends Rabba to investigate and he finds the source: an incident with actions and a response.
Orphans come before Rava, he rules, the Sages challenge him and he justifies it: incident followed by a ruling.
The Sidon tanner incident with the Sages' ruling is a story, though it is the Mishnah's own copy (R-C1).
A woman writes her property to her daughter, marries and is divorced: the opening of a narrated incident with several actions.
Orphans come before Rava, he rules, the Sages challenge him and he justifies it: incident followed by a ruling.
Funeral costs drove relatives to flee; Rabban Gamliel had himself buried in linen and everyone followed: a one-time act with a response and a change.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi tricks the Angel of Death, jumps into paradise and meets Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai: a full narrative.
A remedy plus a bare one-line report that Rav Shimi bar Ashi used it and the patient was healed, cited as evidence.
A man has ten write a get, the signing is delayed, he comes before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who rules: incident plus ruling.
Wondrous incidents (the mustard branch breaks, nine kav found, its wood used for a booth) narrated as events; the eyewitness-wonder type he has accepted.
A man sets a 30-day get condition, is held up by the ferry, shouts across the river, and Shmuel rules: incident plus ruling.
A habitual practice (the maidservants would sing to Rabbi Abbahu) with no one-time event following.
Rabbi Hanina declines the appointment, Rabbi Afes dies, Levi goes to Babylonia and Rav deduces it: a narrative chain of events.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba meets Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi hurrying his grandson to school, asks why, and changes his own practice from then on.
Ulla dies abroad, they tell Rabbi Elazar, he laments, they say the coffin is coming, he answers: an event with responses.
Rabba bar bar Hana brings a partly unwitnessed get and comes before Rabbi Elazar, who rules: incident plus ruling.
A yevama case set up as an incident, but the passage is mostly negotiation between the brothers: speech with conflict and no resolution in the passage.
A legal discussion of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on nursing vows; no narrated event.
A legal ruling with an incident only alluded to in one line (a woman strangled her child) as evidence; not narrated.
A man makes a deal with his sharecropper, rain comes, and Rav Yosef and Rabba rule: incident plus ruling.

Rabbi's matchmaking: the girl dies, lineage is investigated, a new match is made, the son studies twelve years, the wife becomes infertile and is healed through prayer. A chain of events with consequences.
Rav Beivai's request to remove the ladder is a brief report of conduct cited to challenge Rabba's ruling; nothing follows and the rest is legal discussion.
Pure legal discussion about the grooms' benediction; Boaz is cited only as a scriptural source.
Incidents of 'a certain man' betrothing with low-value items that rabbis assessed; in the second the mother objects and Rav Hisda answers her. Incident plus ruling, with a response.
A legal dilemma, then Rav Nahman's rhetorical jab at Rav Anan inside the argument. Speech only, with no event.
Rabbi Yohanan's relatives consult him and then Reish Lakish, who threatens them; they return to Rabbi Yohanan, who concedes. Events, conflict and a resolution.
Homa comes before Rava, her arm is exposed, Rava goes home, and his wife drives Homa out of Mehoza. A full narrative.
A dialogue in which the son corrects his father's teaching and Shmuel rebukes the son. Mostly speech, but with conflict.
First-person eyewitness wonders ('once I rose early and walked in honey'). This is the open eyewitness-wonder category the expert accepted for Ketubot 111b.
Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai meets Nakdimon's impoverished daughter; the encounter, dialogue, recognition and his weeping form a full story.
Two Rabbi Meir stories: he stops the steward despite a dream, and he makes peace between quarrelers, after which Satan is heard lamenting.
Halakhic statements and resolutions about educating children; Abaye's mother's sayings are teachings, not events.
The Gemara quotes the Mishnah incident of a get brought before Rabban Gamliel, which he validated. Incident plus ruling, and the expert said this Gittin 10b quotation can be included.
Legal reasoning about teruma; no event.
Dama ben Netina, a post-biblical gentile, forgoes a huge profit rather than wake his father. A one-time event, and in scope.
After a habitual frame (Hillel provided a horse and servant), a one-time event follows: one time he ran before the pauper for three mil himself.
Bar Tzartzur's heirs come before Rav Amram, ignore him, are threatened and sent to Rav Nahman, who rules. Incident, conflict and a ruling.
A man complains to Rabban Gamliel, the bride explains, he investigates her relatives and rules. Incident, investigation and resolution.
First-person incidents: food was brought to Shmuel and Rav Kahana, and each gave some to the attendant, who would otherwise have been endangered. Something happened and a person responded.
A description of Rabbi Abba's habitual charity practice, with no one-time event.
Cases of 'a certain man' whose bequest changed in value, followed by a rabbinic ruling: the incident-plus-ruling shape of R-C0, though minimal.
Kamtza and bar Kamtza is a full narrative. Rabbi Yohanan's closing comment in segment 8 is commentary and is excluded.
The Gemara's commentary on the Mishnah's innkeeper story, filling in details to resolve a legal issue. It is not itself the story.
Statements about atonement plus a report of how long Rabba and Abaye lived, with no narrated incident.
An incident: Rabbi rules, Perata challenges him, and Rabbi reverses (or refrains), told in two versions. Action, conflict and change.
A widow comes before Rabba bar Rav Huna, is refused, curses him, and he overturns his chair yet still suffers weakness: events, conflict and consequence.
The Gemara's explanation of what Rabbi Akiva was thinking; commentary on a reported act, not a narrative.
A legal statement about conditional divorces for soldiers with a verse exegesis; no narrated event.
A list of folk beliefs ending with a bare report about Shapur's daughter being placed among spices; nothing follows, no conflict.
Rav Hiyya bar Abba's child dies; Reish Lakish comes the next day with his disseminator who speaks words of 'comfort': a narrated incident with actions and tension.
Rav Kahana taking a cloth and Mar bar Rav Ashi buying one are bare reports of practice cited as halakhic evidence, with nothing following.
A sharecropper betroths a woman with onions and comes before Rava, who rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
Ravina finds Mar bar Rav Ashi braiding a garland and challenges him; mostly a halakhic exchange with mild conflict and little action.
Rabbi Yohanan's relatives come to him, he advises them, and he later regrets acting as a legal advisor: incident, response and change.
A creditor seizes an ox from the orphans' herdsman, they dispute, and Rav Nahman rules: incident followed by a ruling.
A fragment of exegetical argument about Joshua 5:11; no narrative.
Silk deposited with Rav Dimi, who dies without instruction; the claimant comes before Rabbi Abba, who rules: incident plus ruling.
Rav Nahman's relative sells her ketubah, is divorced and dies; purchasers claim from her daughter and Rav Nahman responds: a sequence of events with conflict.
Rabbi Tarfon recounts a one-time occasion when he ascended the platform, inclined his ear and heard the High Priest conceal the Name; a first-person eyewitness incident, though thin.
Ze'eiri avoids Rabbi Yohanan's marriage offer; one day he carries him across water and Rabbi Yohanan confronts him: actions and conflict.
Mar Yehuda challenges two scholars, they fall silent, go to Rabba who rebukes the questioner; mainly scholastic dialogue with some conflict.
Rav Minyumi's eyewitness account of a woman claiming a tenth of the estate before Ameimar, her brothers' response and Ameimar's silence: an incident with a judicial response.
Rabbi Hanina declines the headship, sits outside with Levi; Rabbi Afes dies, Levi leaves for Babylonia and Rav deduces it: a chain of events.
A bare report that Bonyam ben Nunyam sent Rabbi fabrics, used only to explain a word; nothing follows.
Rabbi Pinhas plans an escape, makes his statements, is carried off and pursued, and the investigation is abandoned: a full narrative.
Men drown, bodies are recovered after days, and Rav Dimi and Rava permit the wives to remarry: incidents followed by rulings.
A Mehoza woman married in Neharde'a comes before Rav Nahman, who recognizes her accent, rules, is challenged and reverses: incident with ruling and change.
A habitual practice of Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai with no one-time event following, embedded in halakhic discussion.
Purely legal analysis of the difference between two opinions; no narrative.
Rav Pappa reports a teaching and Rav Shimi gives a variant tradition; a transmission of a teaching through speech without conflict.
A man comes before Rabbi Ami with testimony, is questioned, and Rabbi Ami acts by elevating the person to the priesthood: an incident followed by a ruling.
Rabbi Abbahu's dictum embeds an incident: Rabbi Hanina ben Gamliel's fearful household tried to feed him a limb from a living animal; the Gemara identifies and clarifies the event.
Rav Pappa serves drinks at his son's wedding, a guest fails to stand, and Rav Pappa becomes angry: an event with an emotional reaction.
Exegetical teaching with a scholarly challenge by Rabbi Hiyya; speech only, no narrated event or real conflict.
A pauper comes to Rava, they dispute, and Rava's sister arrives with exactly the food in question, leading Rava to concede: events with conflict and resolution.
A man bequeaths property to Toviya, dies, Toviya arrives, and Rabbi Yohanan rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
A man rents a millstone, grows rich, buys his own, and a dispute arises over payment: a narrated incident with conflict.
A widow suing orphans dresses in all her clothes at their request, and Ravina rules on the case: incident followed by a ruling.
Rabba bar bar Hana recounts seeing an Arab woman spinning who throws down her spindle and addresses him, and Rav Ukva comments: a one-time event with actions and response.
A man leaves Pumbedita and Rav Yosef excommunicates him; another leaves and dies, prompting Abaye's remark: incidents with responses.
Nero, a post-biblical figure, tests his fate with arrows and a child's verse, then flees and converts: a full narrative.
Two deeds come before Rav Yosef, he rules, and the losing party argues with him: a court incident; segment 6 is the Gemara's own resolution.
Rav Yehuda's habitual practice and Ulla's advice; speech without conflict and no one-time event.
Judges rule, Reish Lakish reverses their decision, and Rabbi Yohanan criticizes him: actions with conflict.
A man complains to Rabban Gamliel, who answers with a suspicious question and a parable; mostly dialogue, with implied conflict and no further action.
Rav Pappa goes to write his son's marriage contract, Yehuda bar Mareimar comes to greet him and takes leave at the door: actions setting up a story.
Habitual practices of Rabbi Yohanan and Rava cited as evidence of a halakha, with no one-time event.
A woman comes before Rav Nahman seeking a divorce, argues, and he rules that the husband is forced: incident with conflict and ruling.
Ravina recites the blessing at betrothal, confident the family won't retract, and they retract: event with reversal.
The Sages reverse the opinions and send a question to Rav, who answers with a vehement oath; quasi-speech acts with conflict.
Shmuel's maidservant is captured, redeemed and sent back with a message: a narrated incident leading to a ruling.
A divorce agent finds the wife kneading, she appoints him her agent, and the case is disputed and sent to Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba; segment 6 is the Gemara's conclusion.
A beautiful woman claims she is betrothed to fend off suitors, later betroths herself, and explains herself to the Sages: a full incident.
Rabbis redeem captives, one is pregnant by a gentile, and Rabbi Ami rules; Rav Yosef's later debate is halakhic discussion, not the story.
Heirs claim a bag of documents from a woman, she claims seizure, and Rav Nahman rules: incident followed by a ruling.
A situation (ruinous funerals, people abandoning their dead) is met by Rabban Gamliel's action, and everyone follows him: an event with a response and a change.
Rabbi Natan asks Sumakhos a question and gets an answer. That is speech only, with no conflict and no event.
Rav Asi's senile mother, his move to Eretz Yisrael, his consultations, and her coffin arriving: a full narrative with actions and a turn.
A report of Rabbi Tarfon's instruction at a halitza, cited as evidence for a derivation. Nothing follows from it.
The widow sues the orphans, they object to her dress, she dresses up, and Ravina rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
Bare reports of how many blessings Levi and Rav Asi recited at weddings, cited as practice, with no development.
A man wills a dowry to his daughter, its cost drops, and Rav Idi bar Avin rules on the difference: a real incident resolved by a ruling.
The passage opens an incident ('a certain man who was selling'), which goes on to a woman's request and Rav Hama's ruling. The passage holds the story's beginning.
Solomon, Benayahu and Ashmedai: a full narrative about biblical figures, ruled out of scope by the expert.
The sages visit Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas, are received, ask about the rival wife, and Rabbi Akiva then meets Yonatan: a full narrative. Segment 12 is the Gemara's halakhic explanation and is excluded.
Mostly halakhic dialogue: Abaye challenges Rav Dimi, who falls silent and then praises him. Speech with conflict and no real action.
A man sells land to Rav Pappa, then no longer needs the money, and Rav Pappa gives the land back: an event with a response.
Ravin states a ruling and Rav Hisda rebukes it sharply. Speech only, but with conflict.
A bead seller and a woman exchange words about betrothal, and Rav Hama rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
Ilfa hangs himself from a ship's mast and issues a challenge, and an old man comes and tests him: action, conflict and a response.
A halakhic query, a search through sources and a sent ruling. Quasi-speech acts with no narrative event or conflict.
The incident is only alluded to (a debtor who hid money behind a gentile, and the Sages acted against him). Not enough of it is given.
The heirs come before Rav Amram, ignore his advice, are threatened with excommunication, and are sent to Rav Nahman: incident, conflict and ruling.
A report of Rav's habitual practice of sustaining orphan girls, followed by analysis. Nothing follows from the practice.
Peleimu's habitual taunt is the frame for a one-time event: Satan comes as a pauper, fakes his death, and Peleimu flees. A full narrative.
A report that Rabbi Zeira was avoiding Rav Yehuda, followed at once by Rav Yehuda's dictum. Nothing happens and the narrative goes nowhere.
A bare report of Rav Zevid's ruling or practice, cited as precedent, with no development.
Rav Amram the Pious, the captive women, the ladder, his cry of fire, and the evil inclination leaving him: a full narrative.
Two rabbis on the road see men sowing diverse kinds and argue over whether to ostracize them. Mostly speech, with conflict and minimal action.
Rabbi Hanina declines the headship, Rabbi Afes dies, Levi moves to Babylonia, and Rav deduces it: a narrative. Segment 4 is the Gemara's commentary and is excluded.
A certain man sold his property to go to Eretz Yisrael and did not go; Rav Ashi rules on the sale. An incident followed by a ruling.
A narrated incident (creditor repossesses one mansion, purchaser offers a thousand) with rabbinic rulings in response; the later question about the document is legal discussion.
Rabbi Akiva and Ben Kalba Savua's daughter: betrothal, banishment, twelve years of study, return - a full narrative.
A certain man betrothed a minor with vegetables in the market, and Ravina ruled on it: an incident followed by a ruling.
Shmuel on the ferry: a man helps him, it turns out he has a case, and Shmuel disqualifies himself. An event and a response.
Incident of four sisters in Tzippori whose sons died after circumcision; the fourth came before Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who ruled.
Rav Sheizevi is laughed at and Rava rebukes the mockers - all speech, but there is conflict.
A baraita's laws and the Gemara's analysis; no narrated event.
The incident is only alluded to, to explain the source of a ruling; not enough of it is given.
A report of what Rav Kahana did with an orphan's beer and why, cited as his practice; nothing follows.
A man snatches a belt from a woman, proposes, she takes it back in silence, and Rav Nahman rules: an incident followed by a ruling.
A man passes bareheaded, Ravina reacts, and Rabbi Yirmeya defends him. An event with responses.
A bare report of rulings by Rabbi and Rabbi Hiyya, with no narrative.
Yeimar bar Hashu's agent seizes the boat, and the rabbis confront him and seize it themselves - a narrated incident.
The creditor repossesses one mansion and the purchaser confronts him with a thousand dinars - a narrated incident.
A Mishnah law about consecrating a wife's earnings; no event.
Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok's account of olives sent to Rabbi Yohanan HaHorani, his refusal, and the father's reply. The Mishnah citation and the Gemara's inference are commentary.
Hypothetical legal dilemmas; nothing happened.
A gentile announces Hivvai's death offhandedly and Rav Yosef lets his wife remarry: an incident followed by a ruling (twice).
A Roman proposes to a woman, makes her ill with pomegranates, then cures her. A post-biblical narrative with actions and change.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov falls ill, is hung from the cedar column and is healed, then reflects on it - an event with an outcome.
Abaye's tenant farmer asks, Abaye permits it, Rav Yosef corrects him, and Abaye runs after the farmer without catching him.
A woman came to Jerusalem with a child, raised him, he had relations with her, and the court stoned them: an incident and its consequence.
Rav Ami's ruling, an objection and his reply: a legal exchange in speech, with no incident and no real conflict.
At King Izgur's door, Rav Ashi feeds Mar Zutra the king's food, is challenged, and leprosy is found where he points. A full narrative.
Dama ben Netina, a post-biblical gentile, gives up a sale so as not to wake his father and is later rewarded with a red heifer. Several actions, cause and outcome.
A certain man comes before Rav Nahman with a claim about his wedding night, and Rav Nahman orders him flogged. An incident followed by a ruling.

R. Elazar b. R. Yosei testifies once and the court nearly elevates a slave to the priesthood on his word. The testimony has a consequence. The Gemara's emendation is commentary woven into the account.
A halakhic dispute between Rav and Shmuel about a hypothetical case. No event is narrated.
